data.text/markdown:
Explanations in your language

A local explanation says why the model predicted this for this person. The reader of that text may not read English. The argument language= of explain_instance asks the LLM to write the three explanations in the language of the reader. It is one string, and it works with every audience. What you learn here:
  1. The facts do not depend on the language. Python computes them, and the LLM only puts them in words.
  2. How to name a language, and how to use language= with the audiences of the package.
  3. The error that you meet when the key is missing.
What you need: nothing up to the section "Put it in words". After that, you need an LLM. The default model needs OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Each call to the LLM sits behind a button, so you never pay by accident. To use another model, pass model=: see the documentation page "Choosing the model".

The model and the facts

The same Titanic EBM as in the other notebooks: a binary classifier without interactions. Pick a passenger. The facts below come from compute_local_facts and facts_to_texts. Neither function takes a language, because a number is the same in every language. The language only changes the words around the facts.

How to name a language

Pass any name that the LLM knows. The package does not keep a list of languages, so a new language needs no new release. The table shows names that work well:
language= Result
"English" The default.
"French", "German", "Japanese" The name of the language in English. This is the clearest form.
"Deutsch", "日本語" The name of the language in that language.
"Brazilian Portuguese", "Simplified Chinese" A variety of a language, where the variety matters.
"formal German" A language with a register.
The package does not check the name. A misspelt name goes to the LLM as it is, and the LLM may guess the language or answer in English. If the text comes back in the wrong language, check the spelling first. The facts and the numbers stay as they are. The instruction asks the LLM to keep every number and to translate the names of the inputs only where the reader needs them.

Put it in words

Now call the LLM. explain_instance needs the global explanation of the model, computed once with describe_ebm. That is the slow step: one chain per feature, then a summary. The global explanation is written in English here, and the local explanations are not: the argument language= sets the language of the local ones only. If you want the global explanation in another language too, write it in that language and pass it as it is.

One passenger, several languages

Choose the languages and press the button. Each language is one call of explain_instance, which sends three requests. Three languages send nine requests, so keep the list short. The tabs show the three explanations of each language, side by side with the same facts.

data.text/markdown:
The same language, another audience

The language and the audience are two settings, and each one has its own job. The audience decides which facts the LLM gets and how it is told to write for the reader. The language decides the language of the words. So a data scientist who reads Spanish gets the scores of the data scientist, in Spanish. Type any language name below. It does not need to be in the list.
